# Spaced Repetition Field Notes

Spaced repetition distributes review across expanding intervals. The first
review happens soon after learning, the next a day later, then a few days, then
weeks. The goal is to meet each idea just before it would be forgotten, so
recall stays effortful but successful.

Retrieval practice beats rereading. Closing the source and reconstructing an
answer strengthens memory more than passively scanning the same page again. A
short quiz after reading is worth more than a second pass.

Interleaving mixes related topics within one session. Switching between
algebra and geometry, or between two authors, feels harder but improves
transfer. Blocked practice feels fluent and is often mistaken for learning.

Desirable difficulty is the useful middle ground. If review is too easy, it
adds little; if it is too hard, it discourages. Adjusting interval length and
question format is how practitioners tune that middle ground.

Sleep consolidates what was studied. Material reviewed in the evening and again
the next morning sticks better than the same material reviewed twice in one
sitting. Scheduling matters as much as the content.

Coverage matters for a reading queue. Every passage should be visited before
any passage repeats, otherwise the early chapters crowd out the later ones. A
coverage-first policy with a cooldown window keeps the whole source in play.
